notes.meaning: Solomon finished the temple first before spending thirteen years building his royal palace complex. He took longer on his own house because there were fewer materials prepared in advance and no urgent command from God driving the schedule. Building the temple first showed that he put God's honor before his own comfort.

Solomon built a grand hall known as the House of the Forest of Lebanon. It was named for its rows of massive cedar pillars, which made the inside look like a forest of cedar trees. This large building served as an armory for weapons as well as a state hall.

The roof of this hall rested on cedar beams placed across forty-five pillars arranged in three rows. Windows were set in three tiers on opposite walls so that the openings lined up across from each other. All the doorways and doorposts were made with square frames to match the clean design of the windows.

Solomon also built a colonnade, or pillared porch, that was fifty cubits long and thirty cubits wide. It stood in front of the main hall, with a covered porch and steps at the entrance. This colonnade provided a sheltered walkway for guards and visitors who came to the palace on business.

Next to the colonnade, Solomon built the Hall of Justice, where his royal throne stood. The room was lined with cedar wood from floor to ceiling. Here the king sat to hear legal cases and give fair rulings to the people.

Solomon constructed his private living quarters in an inner courtyard behind the judgment hall using the same high-quality workmanship. He also built a similar palace for Pharaoh's daughter, his royal wife. These separate quarters gave the queen a residence fitting her royal status.

All these royal buildings were built with expensive, high-grade stones cut and sawn to exact sizes on both their inner and outer surfaces. The builders laid huge foundation stones, some measuring twelve to fifteen feet in length. On top of these stones, the walls were finished with dressed stonework and cedar beams.

A great courtyard surrounded the entire palace complex, enclosed by a wall made of three courses of cut stone and a row of cedar beams. This wall was built in the same manner as the inner court and porch of the temple. The courtyard gave the people a place to gather and visually tied the king's palace to the house of God.

King Solomon sent to Tyre for a master metalworker named Huram to make the bronze furnishings for the temple. Huram was the son of an Israelite widow from the tribe of Naphtali, and his deceased father had been a bronze craftsman from Tyre. Huram possessed exceptional skill, understanding, and knowledge for all types of metalwork, gifts God gave him to beautify His house.

Huram cast two massive bronze pillars, each standing eighteen cubits tall and twelve cubits around. Because they were so large and thick, casting these hollow bronze columns was an extraordinary feat of metalworking. They stood prominently at the entrance to the temple porch.

Huram made two bronze capitals, or decorative top pieces, to sit on top of the pillars. Each capital was five cubits high and cast in solid bronze. These impressive crowns added extra height and beauty to the top of each pillar.

To decorate the capitals, Huram created ornamental networks of interwoven lattice and chainwork. Seven wreaths of twisted chains were draped around each capital, holding two encircling rows of bronze pomegranates. These carvings reminded the people of the richness and fruitfulness of God's blessing.

The upper section of each capital was carved into the shape of open lily blossoms four cubits high. Just below this lily design, where the capital swelled outward, were two hundred bronze pomegranates arranged in two rows. Together on both pillars, there were four hundred pomegranates displayed on the ornate bronze wreaths.

Solomon set up the two pillars at the entrance to the temple portico. He named the south pillar Jachin, meaning 'He will establish,' and the north pillar Boaz, meaning 'in Him is strength.' These names reminded all who entered to rely completely on God for firmness and spiritual strength.

The very tops of the pillars were finished with delicate lily shapes. With these decorations in place, the work on the two great entrance pillars was complete. Their finished design stood as a sign of purity, strength, and God's faithfulness at the door of the sanctuary.

Huram also cast a massive circular bronze basin known as the Sea. It measured ten cubits from rim to rim, five cubits high, and thirty cubits around. It replaced the smaller washbasin of the tabernacle, holding vast amounts of water for the priests to wash in as they served God.

Directly below the rim of the Sea, two rows of bronze gourds or ornamental buds were cast as part of the bowl itself. There were ten of these carved buds for every cubit around the thirty-cubit perimeter, making three hundred in each row. These decorations were cast in one piece with the basin rather than soldered on afterward.

The great bronze basin rested upon twelve cast-bronze oxen, grouped in threes facing north, west, south, and east. Their hindquarters faced inward toward the center to support the massive weight of the water. The twelve oxen reminded the priests that they were ministering on behalf of all twelve tribes of Israel.

The walls of the bronze Sea were about three inches thick, the width of a man's hand. Its rim curved outward like a drinking cup or an open lily flower, and it could hold two thousand baths, which was thousands of gallons of water. This abundant water supply provided the ceremonial cleansing the priests needed before entering the presence of the Lord.
